First, D\&R's reported advantage over soft reweighting is entirely attributable to multi-epoch exposure; at equal content epochs ($N{=}3$), the two approaches differ by $\Delta{=}0.006$ PPL (Table~\ref{tab:epoch_match}).
Second, dual-constrained exponent selection with minimum intervention consistently outperforms both uniform weighting and the ESS-only alternative across contamination levels ($\rho \in \{0.4, 0.6\}$), with the quality constraint preventing 4.9$\times$ over-aggressive downweighting in 38.2\% of batches.
The adaptive-to-grid gap (0.031 PPL) falls within grid-search's own cross-seed variance ($\pm$0.033, 95\% CI $[-0.039, 0.101]$), reducing search cost from nine runs to one.
Third, detector signal type (discriminative vs.\ generative), not AUC, determines reweighting effectiveness.
The method has clear boundaries: it fails at $\rho{=}0.2$, and at 1.7B we find no evidence of either improvement or degradation ($\Delta{=}{-}0.01$, 2 seeds), suggesting its primary value lies in the moderate-scale continued pretraining regime tested here.
Future work: multi-seed scale experiments, discriminative detector characterization across architectures, and evaluation on naturally contaminated corpora.
Code and data will be released upon acceptance.

Detect-and-reweight methods suppress likely-synthetic samples during pretraining via $w(x) = (1-q(x))^b$, where $q(x)$ is a detector's synthetic probability.
Two questions are open: does hard filtering (Detect and Remove, D\&R) outperform soft reweighting, and how should $b$ be set without per-model grid search?

We address both through controlled experiments in a self-contamination setting: Qwen3-0.6B continued pretraining on 132M FineWeb tokens with 40\% synthetic contamination (3 seeds).
First, D\&R's reported advantage is entirely a multi-epoch artifact: at equal content epochs, reweighting and D\&R differ by only 0.006 PPL ($N{=}3$).
Second, a dual-constrained adaptive exponent $b^*$ that selects the minimum $b$ satisfying a quality floor and stability ceiling improves over uniform weighting with directional consistency across all seeds; adaptive $b^*$ performs comparably to grid-best (95\% CI of the gap includes possible degradation up to 0.10 PPL).
Third, our results suggest that detector signal type may matter more than discrimination accuracy: two generative detectors both reverse the advantage that a discriminative classifier provides (3 detectors, single seed).

The method fails at low contamination ($\rho{=}0.2$), establishing a clear applicability boundary.
$N{=}3$ precludes formal significance testing; we report effect sizes and directional consistency.
